# Risk Briefs {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Four briefs, five-minute slots (four minutes + one question)

Each brief follows the same four steps, so that the room can compare them: what happened, what it means, which channel reaches a firm, and what to do.

| | |
|---|---|
| **0–1** | The development |
| **1–3** | The view |
| **3–4** | The exposure — which channel? |
| **4–5** | The recommendation, and its trigger |

::: {.muted}
One question per brief today. Hard stop at six minutes.
:::

# What an economic order is {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Three questions describe any order

An **international order** is a set of rules, institutions and expectations governing relations between states, backed by some distribution of power. The **economic order** is the part that governs trade, money and investment.

| Question | Look at |
|---|---|
| **Who wrote the rules?** | Which states designed the institutions, in whose interest |
| **What do the rules say?** | Openness to trade, capital, investment; dispute settlement |
| **What holds them in place?** | Hegemonic power · shared interest · institutional momentum |

Use the three questions as a checklist for any order, past or present: today's session applies them to the post-1945 order; Session 03 asks what happens to the third when power shifts.

::: {.get}
The multinational lives inside the economic order without noticing — until it changes.
:::

# The post-1945 order {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Four layers {.scrollable}

| Layer | When | What it did |
|---|---|---|
| **Bretton Woods** | 1944 | IMF and IBRD; fixed but adjustable rates, dollar anchored on gold |
| **GATT** | 1947 | Tariff-cutting rounds; most-favoured-nation; national treatment |
| **Embedded liberalism** | 1950s–70s | Openness abroad, protection and autonomy at home (Ruggie 1982) |
| **Neoliberal turn and WTO** | 1971–2001 | Gold link ends; capital opens; WTO 1995 with binding disputes, TRIPS, TRIMs; China joins 2001 |

::: {.muted}
Read the layers as a sequence of bargains, not one design. The early order managed openness — capital controls were normal and free trade was managed — so that it stayed politically sustainable at home. The later layers opened capital and reached into services, intellectual property and investment, with rulings that bind.
:::

## Easy to join, hard to overturn

> The American-led order was open, rule-based and institutional enough that rising states gain more by joining than by challenging it.

::: {.muted}
Ikenberry, G. J. (2011). *Liberal Leviathan*. Princeton UP.
:::

This is the liberal answer to the third question — what holds the rules in place. On this view, institutions have a momentum of their own: a rising power such as China, which joined the WTO in 2001, gains more from the rules than it would from overturning them.

::: {.step}
Session 03 sets the realist reply beside it: orders reflect power, and change when power does.
:::

# Baldwin's three unbundlings {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Three costs

Baldwin organises globalisation around the cost of moving three things. Each time one of them falls, production can be split from something it used to be tied to.

::::: columns

:::: {.column width="33%"}

### Goods

Steam, railways, steamships. Fell from the 19th century: things could be made far from where they were bought.

::::

:::: {.column width="33%"}

### Ideas

Telecoms, the internet. Fell from about 1990: a factory abroad could be coordinated from headquarters.

::::

:::: {.column width="33%"}

### People

Still expensive. Telepresence may change that, by separating the worker from the workplace.

::::

:::::

::: {.muted}
Baldwin, R. (2016). *The Great Convergence*. Belknap / Harvard UP.
:::

## Divergence, then convergence {.scrollable}

| | Cheap to move | Unbundled | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| **First unbundling** | goods | production from consumption | Industry clusters in the North → **great divergence** |
| **Second unbundling** | ideas | the factory itself | Know-how moves South **inside value chains** → **great convergence** |
| **Third (prospective)** | people, virtually | worker from workplace | Competition by task and occupation |

In the first unbundling, ideas still moved cheaply only within a region, so industry stayed clustered where it began. In the second, stages of production could be offshored while know-how travelled with them, inside firms.

::: {.get}
In the second unbundling, **the multinational is the vehicle of convergence**. Technology, jobs and security dependence now travel together — through the supply chain. That is why geopolitics now reaches firms so directly.
:::

## Baldwin's evidence — today's target

::: {.step}
The **G7 share of world GDP**: rising for a century, then falling sharply from around 1990.
:::

- Almost all of the gain goes to a few economies — Baldwin's **Industrialising Six**: China, Korea, India, Poland, Indonesia, Thailand
- Ask of the figure: **which dollars?** Current, constant, PPP?
- Note also that the **G7 is not in the data**: the World Bank publishes no G7 aggregate, so you build it by summing the seven members

The turning point coincides with the fall in the cost of moving ideas — that is Baldwin's argument in one picture.

::: {.muted}
You rebuild it in the practice round — and then rebuild it at PPP.
:::

# From convergence to backlash {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Rodrik's trilemma {.scrollable}

A country can have at most **two** of deep economic integration, national sovereignty and democratic politics. Each row is one way of choosing.

| Keep | Give up | Looks like |
|---|---|---|
| integration + sovereignty | democracy | the golden straitjacket |
| integration + democracy | sovereignty | global federalism |
| sovereignty + democracy | **deep integration** | Bretton Woods compromise |

The golden straitjacket means policies dictated by markets; global federalism means rules made above the state; the Bretton Woods compromise means shallow, managed openness.

::: {.get}
Brexit, tariff wars, industrial policy, export controls, "de-risking": choices of sovereignty and democracy over integration.
:::

::: {.muted}
Rodrik, D. (2011). *The Globalization Paradox*. W. W. Norton.
:::

## Slowbalisation

- World trade in % of GDP climbs from the 1990s to **2008**, then broadly **flattens**
- Retreat — or a change of form, from goods to services and data?

A retreat would show up as reshoring and shorter supply chains; a change of form would show up as goods trade stagnating while services and data flows — poorly measured in trade statistics — keep growing. The *extend* step of the practice round lets you see the flattening and judge it.

::: {.step}
When the writers of the rules produce a much smaller share of the world, two questions follow:
**will the rules be rewritten?** (Session 03) · **will the world split into blocs?** (Session 04)
:::

# What it means for the multinational {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Four implications {.scrollable}

| | |
|---|---|
| **Markets are no longer where the rules are written** | Growing revenue in states that did not design the WTO |
| **The supply chain is a geopolitical object** | What the second unbundling moved, export controls now try to stop |
| **Multilateral protection is weaker** | The WTO Appellate Body cannot hear appeals since December 2019 |
| **Measurement is strategy** | Market rates vs PPP: two different boards, two different plants |

::: {.muted}
Each row turns a fact about the order into an item for a firm's risk register. The third is the most concrete: a panel ruling can now be appealed "into the void" and never become binding, so a discriminatory measure by a trading partner is more likely to be settled by bargaining or retaliation between governments than by a legal ruling.
:::

## Put it to the room

> You brief a board deciding where to build a plant. The G7 share at market rates and at PPP tell different stories. **Which do you show, and why?**

::: {.fragment}
::: {.check}
It depends on the decision: **market rates** for purchasing power to buy what you export; **PPP** for the real size of local production and markets.
:::

At market rates the G7 still looks large; at PPP it looks much smaller, because many goods and services are cheaper in lower-income economies. A firm that shows its board only one of the two has made a strategic choice without stating it.
:::

# What the figure does not license {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Four limits

1. A falling share is **relative** — the G7 kept growing; its market did not shrink
2. In **current dollars**, part of every move is the exchange rate — when the dollar strengthens, others shrink in dollar terms without producing less
3. Convergence is **concentrated** — above all in China; "the South" did not converge
4. It shows **income**, not **rule-making power**

Each limit is a conclusion a reader might draw from the chart and that the data do not support — the template for today's catch.

::: {.warn}
That last one is a question for Session 03, not a reading of this chart.
:::

# The Tableau skill of the day {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Pivot, then share

DataBank gives you **years as columns**; Tableau wants **one row per country-year**. Pivoting turns the wide table into a long one.

1. Data source pane → select all year columns → right-click → **Pivot**
2. Rename: `Pivot Field Names` → `Year`, `Pivot Field Values` → `Value`
3. `Value` → *Number (decimal)*: DataBank's `..` become nulls
4. Calculated field: G7 GDP ÷ World GDP — filter the members on ISO codes, never on names, which are spelt differently from one source to the next ("Korea, Rep.")
5. Check it with **Quick Table Calculation → Percent of Total**

::: {.check}
Over to the practice round: team formation first, then rebuild the G7 share.
:::
